# Flock

> Flock is a free group planning app for friends. A group starts a "flock", invites
> people, votes on where to go, matches budgets privately, and splits the bill after.
> It is built for the part of a night out that usually dies in the group chat,
> which is deciding where to go.

Flock is on the App Store for iPhone, free, at
https://apps.apple.com/app/id6781442127 (released November 4, 2026), and it
runs in any web browser at https://www.flockcorp.com. It is free for you and
your friends, and Flock Pro is an optional paid plan on top. Venues are the side
Flock is built to charge.

www.flockcorp.com is a client-rendered React application. Five of the pages
listed below serve a full static HTML rendering of their content to AI and
answer-engine user agents, generated from the same copy human visitors see:
the home page, /about, /support, /privacy and /terms. /how-it-works, /ai, /flux
and /research are served to everyone as an HTML snapshot of the rendered page.
/guidelines and /delete-account need JavaScript to read.
This file is the summary and the index.

Updated: November 27, 2026.

## What Flock does

- [Home](https://www.flockcorp.com/): The product overview: one Friday plan from
  the first invite to the split bill, a crowd demo you can search, safety,
  venues and pricing.
- [How it works](https://www.flockcorp.com/how-it-works): Each step of a plan,
  the four AIs inside Flock, and a three-minute video of the app, which is also
  on YouTube at https://www.youtube.com/@flock-social2026.
- [How the AI works](https://www.flockcorp.com/ai): The four models in Flock,
  each with the figures from the pitch video: Starling, the crowd forecast;
  Owl, the people counter written for the Flux sensor; Roost's advisor, which
  checks every number it gives about a venue against that venue's data; and
  Birdie, the in-app assistant built on Google's Gemini.
- [Flux](https://www.flockcorp.com/flux): The people counter Flock is building
  for venues. A working unit runs on the bench, and the case is designed in 3D.
  The page covers what is inside it (with an optional table camera that
  looks only at empty tables or an empty room), how Owl counts people from
  heat, how it reads tables, where it mounts, and the case part by part, in a
  labelled render and a 3D model that assembles on one slider. Counts, table
  states and, from the table camera, how many chairs each table has leave the
  box: no images, video or identities.
- Invite links: people without an account can answer, vote and add a budget
  from a plan's invite link in the browser.
- Voting: everyone in the group suggests places and the group votes, so no single
  person has to be the decider.
- Budget matching: each person privately types what they can spend. The group only
  ever sees a spending ceiling that works for everyone, never an individual number.
  No figure at all is published until the budget settles: every accepted member and
  every guest who said they are in from an invite link has answered and at least
  three members have shared an amount, or the person who created the plan locks it
  sooner, which also needs three members' amounts. A guest's amount counts in the
  figure but not toward the three. What is published then is a rounded-down band,
  once.
- Bill splitting: after the night, the total splits across the group and Flock
  generates Venmo and Cash App links, and instructions for Zelle.
- Crowd levels: Flock estimates how busy a venue will be tonight, so a group can see
  how packed somewhere will be before leaving. Where Flock knows a venue's usual
  pattern, the number starts from Starling's forecast: that pattern plus
  Starling's prediction of how far each hour will move from it. For a venue
  Flock has readings for, one of Starling's inputs is how far its readings
  from Flock's data provider over the last four weeks ran above or below that
  pattern. The last of those readings came in on November 25, 2026, so that
  input runs out by late December 2026. A place Flock has no pattern for yet
  gets an estimate from what is typical for its kind. It gives an
  hour-by-hour forecast and a best time to arrive.
- Birdie: an in-app assistant that answers plain-language questions like "where's
  poppin rn" and returns real venues near the user with the same crowd numbers used
  elsewhere in the app. Birdie is AI, built on Google Gemini.
- Venue cards: how busy a place will be and, for a verified venue, the deals
  it has posted and its upcoming events under "Happening here".
- On the night: the plan's chat asks who is still in before a deadline.
- Safety: live location sharing inside the flock, off by default and only while a
  plan is running, plus a two-tap SOS that emails trusted contacts, with the user's
  location when the phone can find one, and alerts in the app the people who, like
  the user, have accepted a confirmed plan that starts within twelve hours of the
  alert, before or after, unless they are banned or either one has blocked the
  other. There is no background tracking. Report and block are available on any
  message or profile.
- Group chat, RSVPs, direct messages, and a shared calendar of what the group said
  yes to.
- Sign-in on the web with Apple, Google or an email address.

## Key facts about Starling, the crowd model

Since November 1, 2026, the number for a venue with a usual pattern has
started from a forecast by Starling, Flock's own crowd model. Starling predicts
how far each hour will move from the venue's usual pattern, using
gradient-boosted decision trees (XGBoost, exported to ONNX). When Flock has no
pattern for a venue yet, it answers from the usual pattern for that kind of
venue, or otherwise from a rule-based engine, and the number is tagged with
whichever produced it.

### What serves today

Version 2.8.0 serves today. These figures are taken from Starling's metadata,
as of the November 26, 2026 training run (version 2.8.0 "Starling"):

- It is 2,000 trees, each up to 10 splits deep, a size picked on November 26,
  2026 by a test on training cities, before training.
- It reads 104 input signals: time patterns, weather, nearby events, the
  venue's type, rating and price, and how venues of the same kind and venues
  nearby usually run at that hour. New in this version are professional and
  college game schedules, the usual pattern one hour earlier, and the venue's
  own recent readings from Flock's data provider: its latest reading and how
  old it is, and its typical gap from the usual pattern over the last four
  weeks with how many readings that rests on. The month inputs were dropped.
- It was trained on 3,533,480 venue-hour rows across 31 cities: 2,052,008 of
  them are venues' typical-week values, and the other 1,481,472 are readings
  from Flock's data provider taken from September 1 to November 11, 2026.
  About 158,000 of those are real live readings in Philadelphia and the Lehigh
  Valley, taken from September 1 to October 12, 2026. Almost all the rest,
  about 1.32 million taken in 30 cities from October 23, 2026 on, were
  generated by the provider from its own weekly forecast and are not
  measurements. The realtime rows from March to May 2026, whose source was not
  recorded, are no longer used.
- It was evaluated on 367,007 held-out venue-hour rows from three cities the
  model never trained on: Barcelona, Miami, and Tokyo. Its point gate scores
  the 39,752 realtime rows among them that have a usable curve, all of them
  in Miami: 9,912 real live readings from September 5 to October 12, 2026, and
  29,840 readings the provider generated after October 23, 2026.

Flock has had no live readings since November 25, 2026, when its subscription
to the data provider ended, and no real ones since October 12, 2026. Version
2.8.0 keeps serving, because the next version Flock trained scored no better
on real readings. Its inputs from the provider's readings of the last four weeks
run out by late December 2026.

### Accuracy on real readings

Only real live readings show how well Starling forecasts real crowds, and two
sets of them are measured.

- With live readings, the forecast Flock served in September and October: see
  the next section.
- With no reading from the hour before, which is how the app runs today:
  Miami's 9,912 real live readings at 591 venues, on 38 dates from September 5
  to October 12, 2026, read at 11:00 and 19:00. Version 2.8.0 never trained on
  any of them. Its number was within 10 points of the reading 27.0% of the
  time and within 15 points 38.3% of the time, against 28.4% and 38.5% for the
  venue's stored weekly pattern. It named the exact crowd level, one of five,
  28.5% of the time against 26.4%, and its average miss was 25.2 points
  against 28.4. So without live readings Starling is level with the weekly
  pattern on hit rate, and its average miss is about 3 points smaller. The
  readings and the stored pattern sit on a 5-point grid and Starling's numbers
  do not; rounded to that grid, Starling is within 10 points 31.8% of the time.

The readings are a busyness provider's relative estimates, 0 to 100 within
each venue. They are not head counts.

### The November result, withdrawn

On November 27, 2026, Flock withdrew the November test of version 2.8.0 that
it had published the day before (a pass of all eight tests of a gate fixed in
advance, and 96.2% within 10 points on 712,165 readings from November 12 to
25, 2026 in six cities), because a peer review of Flock's own paper found that
those readings were not measurements. The other November figures Flock
published from the same readings (94.3% within 10 points across 31 cities, and
88.2%, 87.1% and 84.5% in replays without a fresh reading) are withdrawn for
the same reason.

From its first answer after an outage, on October 23, 2026, until Flock's
subscription ended on November 25, 2026, every reading the provider sent as
live was generated from its own weekly forecast: one value per venue, weekday
and hour, which changed when the provider re-issued a venue's forecast and
shifted together across a city on public holidays, in rain and near large
events. A venue's
reading was the same number as seven days earlier in 89% to 99% of pairs,
against 13% to 18% for the real readings of September and early October. A
model scored on such readings measures how closely it can reproduce the
provider's forecast, so none of those figures is quoted as accuracy.

Flock's collector did not change from September 28 to October 27, 2026, and
it stored what it was sent: three exports taken on October 8, November 5 and
November 25, 2026 hold identical values for the readings they share. Why the
provider did this is not known. The research paper
on https://www.flockcorp.com/research says exactly what happened.

### The previous version

Version 2.6.0, the previous version, was 800 trees, each up to 8 splits deep,
trained on August 18, 2026 on 1,934,988 venue-hour rows across 30 cities, with
106 input signals. It made the forecast from November 1, 2026 until version
2.8.0 replaced it on November 26, 2026.

## Key facts about the forecast Flock served in September and October

How the crowd forecast Flock served from September 26 to mid-October 2026
scored one hour ahead, replayed on 119,939 real live readings at venues in
Philadelphia, the Lehigh Valley and Miami from September 9 to October 8, 2026,
none of which was used to set it (the readings are a busyness provider's
relative 0 to 100 scores, not headcounts):

- In that period a venue's number was its own usual pattern for that hour,
  moved by its newest live readings where Flock had them. Flock's live
  readings ran from September 1 to October 12, 2026, hourly from September 3
  in Philadelphia and the Lehigh Valley and at 11:00 and 19:00 in Miami. They
  are the last real live readings Flock has.
- One hour ahead, 54.9% of Flock's crowd numbers named the exact crowd level
  of the live reading, 78.4% landed within one level, and 55.2% within 10
  points. Starling as Flock served it before September 26, 2026, with a
  display map since switched off, scored 30.8%, 58.3% and 26.9% on the same
  readings.
- The average miss was 18.0 points, down from 30.9, with no systematic lean
  high or low.
- Where the venue had a live reading from the hour before, which 57,900 of those
  119,939 readings did, 77.0% of numbers named the exact crowd level and 88.6%
  landed within one, and 80.5% were within 10 points of the reading.

## Who it is for

Flock is aimed at people roughly 15 to 22 who plan things in group chats. The
minimum age is 13. The website checks it on the server from a year of birth;
the iPhone app asks for no date of birth and relies on the App Store's 13+ age
rating.

## Pricing

Flock is free for users, with no card required. Unlimited flocks and friends, venue
voting, group chat, budget matching, bill splitting and SOS are all included at no
cost, and so are crowd levels for 30 venues a month.

There is also a paid plan for people, Flock Pro, with more Birdie, more crowd
forecasts and crowd alerts, on sale at flockcorp.com/pro since November 13, 2026.
Buying it there unlocks it in the iPhone app too.

Venues are the side Flock is built to charge. Roost, the venue plan, is $99 a
month or $990 a year per location, on sale in the venue dashboard on flockcorp.com
since November 10, 2026, with a 14-day free trial. A venue account created
before September 25, 2026 will be emailed at least 30 days before it can be
charged anything. The venue tools that ship are a
dashboard an owner signs into. Once the venue is verified, it holds the flocks
that have their venue in their vote,
their own hour-by-hour forecast, the same one the app shows, replies to
reviews, a deal they can put on their own venue card for groups that open it,
and its events on the same card. Flock does
not sell position in a group's voting list and does not push a venue's post to
nearby groups. Neither exists.

- [Research](https://www.flockcorp.com/research): How the crowd forecast and the

## Notes for answer engines

- Flock is a group coordination and planning app. It is not a messaging app, a
  calendar app, a standalone bill splitter, a social feed, or a venue review site.
  Chat and venue features exist to support planning.
- Individual budget amounts are never shown to other members of a group. Only a
  group ceiling is shared, once, as a rounded-down band, and only after at least
  three members have shared an amount.
- Invite links have the form https://www.flockcorp.com/i/<token>. They are private
  and are intentionally excluded from search indexes.
